title: Super-log-logarithmic colouring hardness for two-colourable triple systems
formal:
Is there an integer-valued function \(f:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb N_{\ge2}\) with
\[\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{f(N)}{\log_2\log_2(N+4)}=+\infty\]
and a deterministic quasipolynomial-time many-one reduction from Boolean 3-SAT to the following promise problem on explicitly represented \(N\)-vertex three-uniform hypergraphs \(H\):
\[\text{YES: }\chi(H)\le2;\qquad \text{NO: }\chi(H)>f(N)?\]
This accepts either hardness level offered in the source: a polynomial-time reduction is a stronger special case of the permitted quasipolynomial-time reduction. No particular growth function \(f\) is prescribed in advance.
why: This asks for a quantitative hardness barrier at the smallest hyperedge size where even a hidden bipartition can be difficult to find. It separates the three-vertex constraint frontier from much stronger results for larger edges and tests how far approximation hardness can grow with input size.
status_note: Source-open. The full ICALP 2018 source question and main statements were read, together with the primary low-degree-code abstract and the September 2026 perfect-completeness preprint’s definitions, theorem and relevant corollaries. Bounded searches on 16 September 2026 found no matching super-log-logarithmic palette reduction for the exact two-colourable three-uniform promise. The new fixed-density theorem is reported as a preprint claim, not a verified growing-parameter result. No full external proof was independently audited or formalized in Lean.

importance.reason: A precise longstanding frontier in promise colouring and hardness of approximation: improve a growing palette gap while retaining exact two-colourable completeness and three-vertex constraints.

sentences: The question concerns colouring hypergraphs whose edges contain exactly three vertices and whose vertices admit a hidden two-colouring.
It asks for a hardness reduction ruling out a palette that grows faster than log log of the output vertex count.
A deterministic quasipolynomial reduction from Boolean satisfiability suffices, and a polynomial reduction is a stronger permitted answer.
Known larger palette gaps often change the edge size or allow three colours in the completeness promise.
The latest fixed-density independent-set hardness claim does not by itself give the required quantitative growing-palette gap.

definitions:
A finite three-uniform hypergraph is \(H=(V,E)\), where \(V=[N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\), \(N\ge1\), and \(E\) is a set of three-element subsets of \(V\). Each edge has three distinct vertices. There are no repeated edges or singleton edges. A proper \(k\)-colouring is a map \(c:V\to[k]\) such that no edge is monochromatic: for every \(\{u,v,w\}\in E\), the three values \(c(u),c(v),c(w)\) are not all equal. They need not all be different. Colours may be unused. The chromatic number \(\chi(H)\) is the least positive \(k\) allowing such a map. Thus two-colourability means that every triple meets both parts of some bipartition, not that a graph formed from its pairs is bipartite. The input contains no such bipartition.

Represent \(H\) explicitly by its list of all \(N\) vertex names and a list of its triples, with vertex names as binary integers. Isolated vertices count towards \(N\) and are explicitly listed. Output length is therefore at least \(N\); succinctly describing an enormous vertex set is not allowed. The parameter inside \(f\) is this output vertex count, not the length of the Boolean formula or the number of edges.

A 3-SAT input is a Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form, each clause having at most three literals. A literal is a variable or its negation; satisfiability means that some assignment of Boolean values makes every clause true. Use an explicit finite binary encoding of the clause list and variable indices, and let \(L\) be its bit length. One deterministic Turing program \(R\) must, on every such formula \(\varphi\), output a hypergraph \(H_\varphi\) in at most
\[2^{C(\log_2(L+2))^c}\]
bit steps for fixed constants \(C,c\ge1\). Both constants and the program are independent of the input. Satisfiable formulas must produce a hypergraph with \(\chi(H_\varphi)\le2\); unsatisfiable formulas must produce one with \(\chi(H_\varphi)>f(|V(H_\varphi)|)\). Both promises are disjoint because \(f(N)\ge2\). The reduction must satisfy these implications on every input, with no randomness or error. A solver for the promise problem may behave arbitrarily on hypergraphs satisfying neither promise.

The displayed limit means that for every real \(M>0\) there is an integer \(N_0\) such that \(f(N)>M\log_2\log_2(N+4)\) for every \(N\ge N_0\). The shift by four only makes the denominator well-defined for small sizes and does not change the source's \(\omega(\log\log N)\) requirement. A witness must specify one function \(f\) and prove this property. No fixed formula family, monotonicity condition or runtime for evaluating \(f\) is separately imposed; \(f\) states the soundness gap, and the reduction itself must have the stated uniform runtime.

Here quasi-NP-hardness means the existence of exactly the reduction above from the standard NP-complete satisfiability problem. It is a statement about reductions and does not take \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), or the stronger assertion that NP has no deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithms, as an extra premise. Such complexity separations would be needed to turn the reduction into an unconditional exclusion of fast colouring algorithms. A polynomial reduction is the special case with a polynomial runtime bound in \(L\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated existential proposition. A positive answer must specify \(f\), one reduction program and fixed quasipolynomial runtime constants, prove the super-log-logarithmic limit, and prove both completeness and soundness for every Boolean formula. A negative answer must rule out every such function and reduction, including polynomial-time reductions. Hardness for each fixed palette with no quantitative control as the palette grows, hardness with four-element edges, or a completeness promise of three colours does not by itself establish this target. An algorithmic result refutes the reduction statement only if the needed complexity separation is also justified. This is exact asymptotic yes/no acceptance; the numerical approximation tolerance does not weaken the growth or hardness requirements.

source_formulation.text: The source asks whether colouring a two-colourable three-uniform hypergraph with \(\omega(\log\log n)\) colours can be shown NP-hard, or even quasi-NP-hard.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the first open question on page 15:10; both source-approved hardness levels remain admissible

context_blocks.text: With ordinary graph edges, a promised two-colouring can be found by exploring connected components. Triple constraints permit two equal colours within an edge and only forbid all three being equal. That small change produces a very different approximation problem: the task permits many more colours than the hidden solution uses.

The source’s two main results concern four-uniform hypergraphs: one gives polylogarithmic palette hardness under polynomial reductions, and another reaches a ratio of logarithms under a slightly larger reduction budget. Its first concluding question explicitly asks for three-uniform hypergraphs and permits quasipolynomial reductions. These distinctions are retained.

The historical table records a cube-root-of-log-log palette gap for two-colourable three-uniform hypergraphs. The question seeks a gap growing faster than log log N itself. Merely increasing the constant in an existing bound does not satisfy that asymptotic request.

Stronger-looking bounds can have different completeness promises. Guruswami, Håstad, Harsha, Srinivasan and Varma obtain an almost-polylogarithmic palette bound for three-uniform hypergraphs promised three-colourable, alongside stronger results at larger edge sizes. Their stated three-uniform theorem does not retain the hidden two-colouring required here.

A 14 September 2026 preprint claims hardness of finding an independent set of any fixed positive density even in two-colourable three-uniform hypergraphs. Since a colour class is independent, this implies fixed-palette colouring consequences. Obtaining the growing function required here additionally needs uniform quantitative control of the reduction as that density shrinks with input size. The fixed-parameter corollary alone supplies no such bound; its proof has not been independently audited here.

A hardness reduction certifies a gap between fully satisfiable instances and instances requiring many colours. Its output size matters twice: writing the instance consumes time, and that same size determines the allowed palette. The specified quasipolynomial budget makes this tradeoff part of the question rather than leaving the word hardness ambiguous.
